title: Teagarden's big band and the drunken trumpeter Stirling Bose
summary: He recalls the personnel of Teagarden's band and Jack leaving drunken trumpeter Stirling on the road.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: We can get into some of the bands you worked with after the Army, with Himber and Chester, and who else were you mentioning?
Teagarden
Was that Teagarden's big band or was that one of the eight or nine piece?
No, it was a big band. Three trumpets, three trombones, with him it made four, five saxes.
Do you recall who some of the players were?
I remember two of the trumpet players. One guys name was Snuffy Claus. His brother Charlie, had been with the band just before I joined.
He was a trumpet player, wasn't he?
Right. Charlie left the band the day before I joined up.
There was a little guy that played the jazz solos, a little, tiny man, skinny and most fragile human you would ever want to see and he played beautifully, but this guy--I don't think
I ever saw him sober, he was out of it every moment of the day. His name was Stirling Bowes-- did you ever hear that name?
I don't think so.
Stirling Bowes.
A trumpet jazz player?
He was a Dixieland type player, but so beautifully; oh, he played so beautiful. He was such a pain in the ass otherwise.

We were once on the road driving and I was in the car with Stirling, Jack was--no, Adie was driving and Jack was sitting next to her and Stirling and I were in the back seat and Stirling kept cursing in his drunken stupor and Jack was saying, 'come on, Jack, calm down, there's a woman in the car, have a little respect.' 'Fuck you and fuck her and fuck this and fuck that.' So Jack said, 'Stirling,--now we're on a stretch of road in the South and you can't see anything in front or anything in back, nothing--and Jack said 'if you don't stop that Stirling, I'm going to put

you out of the car." "I don't give a fuck, fuck you, fuck her," and they stopped the car and Jack pulled him out of the car and threw him on the road and they drove off and left him there. I couldn't believe it, and he appeared a couple of days later on the gig. I have no idea how he got there.
He didn't go back after him?
No, he left him there. He left him there and drove hundreds of more miles to the next gig.
I said, "Jack, how can you do that," and he said, "I don't give a god damn; that's as much as I can take from him."
When he showed up he had bruises, he was black and blue and filthy.
Did he drink any less?
No. He never changed, Stirling. He continued the same way.
You had to love the guy because he was so fragile and such a sweet man, a lovely man,
but he was impossible when he got drunk. He couldn't play beyond a certain point of drinking, he couldn't even get a sound out of his instrument.
